messages.content: You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

Please solve this issue: We got our first GDPR erasure request, and it turns out Remove on the user
list doesn't remove anyone — it flips `active` off and scrambles the email,
and everything else stays.

Make it actually erase: nothing of theirs is left anywhere — not a row, not
a stale search hit. One exception: books they created that are shared with
everyone keep working — people are reading those. Take their name off and
byline them "Deleted author".

One wrinkle: most of the requests we owe are people someone already "removed"
the old way — deactivated, email rewritten to `alice-deactivated-<uuid>@...`.
It has to work for them too, and their sign-in log entries sit under the
address they actually signed in with.

Okay, here's my take on those thoughts, tailored for an expert audience:

**Initial Repository Reconnaissance**

Alright, before diving into anything concrete, my first instinct is always a thorough reconnaissance of the repository. I need to get a high-level understanding of the lay of the land. I'm immediately looking for the project structure – how is the code organized, and are there any obvious design patterns or architectural choices at play? The language is critical, of course; I'll be forming initial hypotheses based on that alone. Then, I'll identify the framework – Spring, Django, React, whatever it may be – that will heavily influence my mental model. Understanding the framework will help me to work with the assumptions encoded into the system's design. The database is also a key factor; I'll be looking for clues in the connection strings, schemas, and ORM usage. Are we talking SQL, NoSQL, or something exotic? How is data persistence handled? And finally, the presence and quality of tests will tell me a lot. Are they unit, integration, or end-to-end? What coverage metrics are available? Do they tell a story about the codebase's evolution and maintainability? All of these factors will quickly help me establish an initial framework for understanding the code and prepare for the more advanced stages.

class User < ApplicationRecord
  include Authoring, Role, Transferable

  has_many :sessions, dependent: :destroy
  has_secure_password validations: false

  has_many :accesses, dependent: :destroy
  has_many :books, through: :accesses
  has_many :leaves, through: :books

  after_create :grant_access_to_everyone_books

  scope :active, -> { where(active: true) }
  scope :ordered, -> { order(:name) }

  def current?
    self == Current.user
  end

  def deactivate
    transaction do
      sessions.delete_all
      update! active: false, email_address: deactived_email_address
    end
  end

  private
    def deactived_email_address
      email_address&.gsub(/@/, "-deactivated-#{SecureRandom.uuid}@")
    end

    def grant_access_to_everyone_books
      all_accesses = Book.with_everyone_access.ids.collect { |id| { book_id: id, level: :reader } }
      accesses.insert_all(all_accesses)
    end
end

module Book::Accessable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  included do
    has_many :accesses, dependent: :destroy
    scope :with_everyone_access, -> { where(everyone_access: true) }
  end

  class_methods do
    def accessable_or_published(user: Current.user)
      if user.present?
        accessable_or_published_books
      else
        published
      end
    end

    def accessable_or_published_books(user: Current.user)
      user.books.or(published).distinct
    end
  end

  def accessable?(user: Current.user)
    accesses.exists?(user: user)
  end

  def editable?(user: Current.user)
    access_for(user: user)&.editor? || user&.administrator?
  end

  def access_for(user: Current.user)
    accesses.find_by(user: user)
  end

  def update_access(editors:, readers:)
    editors = Set.new(editors)
    readers = Set.new(everyone_access? ? User.active.ids : readers)

    all = editors + readers
    all_accesses = all.collect { |user_id|
      { user_id: user_id, level: editors.include?(user_id) ? :editor : :reader }
    }

    accesses.upsert_all(all_accesses, unique_by: [ :book_id, :user_id ])
    accesses.where.not(user_id: all).delete_all
  end
end

  before_action :set_book, only: %i[ show edit update destroy ]

    @books = Book.accessable_or_published.ordered

    @book = Book.new
  end

    book = Book.create! book_params
    update_accesses(book)

    redirect_to book_slug_url(book)
  end

    @leaves = @book.leaves.active.with_leafables.positioned

    respond_to do |format|
      format.html
      format.md
    end
  end

  def edit
  end

  def update
    @book.update(book_params)
    update_accesses(@book)
    remove_cover if params[:remove_cover] == "true"

    redirect_to book_slug_url(@book)
  end

  def destroy
    @book.destroy

    redirect_to root_url
  end

  private
    def set_book
      @book = Book.accessable_or_published.find params[:id]
    end

    def set_users
      @users = User.active.ordered
    end

    def ensure_editable
      head :forbidden unless @book.editable?
    end

    def ensure_index_is_not_empty
      if !signed_in? && Book.published.none?
        require_authentication
      end
    end

    def book_params
      params.require(:book).permit(:title, :subtitle, :author, :cover, :remove_cover, :everyone_access, :theme)
    end

    def update_accesses(book)
      editors = [ Current.user.id, *params[:editor_ids]&.map(&:to_i) ]
      readers = [ Current.user.id, *params[:reader_ids]&.map(&:to_i) ]

      book.update_access(editors: editors, readers: readers)
    end

    def remove_cover
      @book.cover.purge
    end
end

class DemoContent
  class << self
    def create_manual(user)
      book = create_book(user)
      load_markdown_pages(book)
    end

    private
      def create_book(user)
        Book.create(title: "The Writebook Manual", author: "37signals", everyone_access: true).tap do |book|
          with_attachment("writebook-manual.jpg") { |attachment| book.cover.attach(attachment) }
          book.update_access(readers: [], editors: [ user.id ])
        end
      end

      def load_markdown_pages(book)
        pages = {}

        Dir.glob(Rails.root.join("app/assets/markdown/demo/*.md")).each do |fname|
          front_matter = FrontMatterParser::Parser.parse_file(fname)

          if front_matter["class"] == "Section"
            load_section(book, front_matter)
          else
            page = load_markdown_page(book, front_matter)
            attach_images(page)
            pages[page.leaf.slug] = page
          end
        end

        book.leaves.pages.each { |leaf| localize_ref_links(leaf.page, pages) }
      end

      def load_markdown_page(book, front_matter)
        book.press(Page.new(body: front_matter.content), title: front_matter["title"]).page
      end

      def load_section(book, front_matter)
        book.press Section.new(body: front_matter.content, theme: front_matter["theme"]), title: front_matter["title"]
      end

      def attach_images(page)
        re = %r{
          \/u\/           # leading portion of path
          (\S+-\w+\.\w+)  # filename including slug and extension
        }x

        body = page.body.content.gsub(re) do |match|
          with_attachment($1) { |attachment| page.body.uploads.attach(attachment) }

          attachment = page.body.uploads.attachments.last
          attachment.analyze

          "/u/" + attachment.slug
        end

        page.update!(body: body)
      end

      def localize_ref_links(page, pages)
        re = %r{
          (\[.+\])              # link title
          \(                    # opening paren
          \/\d+\/[\w-]+\/\d+\/  # leading portion of path
          ([\w-]+)              # leaf slug
        }x

        body = page.body.content.gsub(re) do |match|
          link_title, leaf_slug, anchor = $1, $2, $3
          linked_page = pages[leaf_slug]
          raise "Invalid reference link: #{page_title}" unless linked_page.present?

          url = Rails.application.routes.url_helpers.leafable_slug_path(linked_page.leaf, anchor: anchor, only_path: true)

          "#{link_title}(#{url}"
        end

        page.update!(body: body)
      end

      def with_attachment(filename)
        File.open(Rails.root.join("app/assets/images/demo/#{filename}")) do |file|
          yield io: file, filename: filename
        end
      end
  end
end

module Authentication
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern
  include SessionLookup

  included do
    before_action :require_authentication
    helper_method :signed_in?

    protect_from_forgery with: :exception, unless: -> { authenticated_by.bot_key? }
  end

  class_methods do
    def require_unauthenticated_access(**options)
      allow_unauthenticated_access **options
      before_action :redirect_signed_in_user_to_root, **options
    end

    def allow_unauthenticated_access(**options)
      skip_before_action :require_authentication, **options
      before_action :restore_authentication, **options
    end
  end

  private
    def signed_in?
      Current.user.present?
    end

    def require_authentication
      restore_authentication || request_authentication
    end

    def restore_authentication
      if session = find_session_by_cookie
        resume_session session
      end
    end

    def request_authentication
      session[:return_to_after_authenticating] = request.url
      redirect_to new_session_url
    end

    def redirect_signed_in_user_to_root
      redirect_to root_url if signed_in?
    end

    def start_new_session_for(user)
      user.sessions.start!(user_agent: request.user_agent, ip_address: request.remote_ip).tap do |session|
        authenticated_as session
      end
    end

    def resume_session(session)
      session.resume user_agent: request.user_agent, ip_address: request.remote_ip
      authenticated_as session
    end

    def terminate_current_session
      Current.session&.destroy!
      reset_session
      remove_authentication_cookie
    end

    def authenticated_as(session)
      Current.session = session
      set_authenticated_by(:session)
      set_authentication_cookie(session)
    end

    def post_authenticating_url
      session.delete(:return_to_after_authenticating) || root_url
    end

    def set_authentication_cookie(session)
      cookies.signed.permanent[:session_token] = { value: session.token, httponly: true, same_site: :lax }
    end

    def remove_authentication_cookie
      cookies.delete(:session_token)
    end

    def set_authenticated_by(method)
      @authenticated_by = method.to_s.inquiry
    end

    def authenticated_by
      @authenticated_by ||= "".inquiry
    end
end

module Leaf::Editable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  MINIMUM_TIME_BETWEEN_VERSIONS = 10.minutes

  included do
    has_many :edits, dependent: :delete_all

    after_update :record_moved_to_trash, if: :was_trashed?
  end

  def edit(leafable_params: {}, leaf_params: {})
    if record_new_edit?(leafable_params)
      update_and_record_edit leaf_params, leafable_params
    else
      update_without_recording_edit leaf_params, leafable_params
    end
  end

  private
    def record_new_edit?(leafable_params)
      will_change_leafable?(leafable_params) && last_edit_old?
    end

    def last_edit_old?
      edits.empty? || edits.last.created_at.before?(MINIMUM_TIME_BETWEEN_VERSIONS.ago)
    end

    def will_change_leafable?(leafable_params)
      leafable_params.select do |key, value|
        leafable.attributes[key.to_s] != value
      end.present?
    end

    def update_without_recording_edit(leaf_params, leafable_params)
      transaction do
        leafable.update!(leafable_params)

        edits.last&.touch
        update! leaf_params
      end
    end

    def update_and_record_edit(leaf_params, leafable_params)

        new_leafable = dup_leafable_with_attachments leafable
        new_leafable.update!(leafable_params)

        update! leaf_params.merge(leafable: new_leafable)

        end
      end
    end

    def record_moved_to_trash
      edits.trash.create!(leafable: leafable)
    end

    def was_trashed?
      trashed? && previous_changes.include?(:status)
    end

**GDPR Erasure: A Deep Dive**

Okay, so we've got a GDPR erasure request and the existing "remove" function isn't cutting it. It's time to make this *actually* erase the user's data. I need to ensure **complete** erasure, except for the shared books. The prompt itself is very important, I need to make sure I don't miss anything.

Here's my breakdown of what's involved, focusing on how the data is stored and what needs to happen during the deletion process:

1.  **Current "Remove" Functionality:** The existing `destroy` method in the `UsersController` deactivates the user (sets `active: false`), scrambles the email, and deletes sessions, but does *not* erase data. The UI uses the destroy method, and needs to be updated.

2.  **User Data Inventory:** Let's go table by table.

    *   `users`: This is the main one. The row itself must be deleted. There's a unique index on email and name, so we need to make sure a deleted user can't re-register with the same info, as well as the deactivated user's `email_address` being stored in sign-in events.
    *   `sessions`: These are *dependent* on the user. The `dependent: :destroy` association is good, but it triggers `record_signed_out` via `Session::Auditable`. This creates a `SignInEvent` if the sessions are destroyed via the `dependent: :destroy`, which needs to be avoided (by using `sessions.delete_all` instead). I must make sure this isn't missed, otherwise the deletion can be incomplete.
    *   `sign_in_events`: Here's the catch. These are linked *only* by email address, but the prompt says existing "removed" users are there, with their OLD email. Deactivation changes the user's `email_address` (e.g., `alice@example.com` to `alice-deactivated-<uuid>@example.com`). I have to find *all* `SignInEvent` rows for the *original* email *and* the current email of a user. If the user's still active, only use the current email, but include both emails if the user has been deactivated. That means using `email_address` OR the original email for a *deactivated* user. We need to find the original email, strip the `-deactivated-<uuid>` from the current email address, and consider the original email, and both. I need to make sure to target both cases where the user has been newly 'removed', or where they were previously 'removed'.

**Deep Dive into Leaf Destruction and Search Index Integrity**

Okay, hold on a second! I need to really understand how our `Book` and `Leaf` destruction processes work, especially considering the `Leaf::Searchable` and `Leaf::Editable` concerns. This warrants a thorough trace of all callbacks and foreign key dependencies when we're destroying a `Book` or a `Leaf`.

First, I'm looking at `app/models/leaf/searchable.rb`. There's the familiar pattern: `after_create_commit`, `after_update_commit`, and critically, `after_destroy_commit` handling the search index. Specifically, I'm zeroing in on that `after_destroy_commit :remove_from_search_index, if: :searchable?` and how it interacts with the `Leaf#delegated_type :leafable, ..., dependent: :destroy` setup.

Now, let's trace `Leaf#destroy`. When `book.destroy` is executed, we know:

1.  `Book` has `has_many :leaves, dependent: :destroy`, so each `Leaf` gets destroyed.
2.  Each `Leaf` has `has_many :edits, dependent: :delete_all`. WAIT! The use of `dependent: :delete_all` for `edits` is a major red flag! It skips the `Edit` destroy callbacks, potentially leaving orphaned records if the underlying `leafable` (e.g., `Page`, `Section`, `Picture`, `ActionText::Markdown`, `ActiveStorage` records) data is destroyed. This is existing code, but it's important to verify it's not a source of trouble.
3.  `Leaf` has `delegated_type :leafable, types: Leafable::TYPES, dependent: :destroy` — okay, the default dependent destruction should run `after_destroy` or `before_destroy`. In Rails, `belongs_to ..., dependent: :destroy` triggers `after_destroy`!
    Now, a critical point: when `leaf.destroy` runs within a transaction (like within `transaction do ... end` or a `user.destroy`), things get tricky!
    *   First, the `leaf` row itself is deleted, and the `leafable` (like `Page` and its associated `ActionText::Markdown`) gets destroyed.
    *   THEN, the `after_destroy_commit` callback *executes AFTER* the transaction commits.
    *   Inside `after_destroy_commit`, `remove_from_search_index` runs *if* `searchable?` is true.
    *   Now, what does `searchable?` do? It calls `searchable_content`.
    *   And `searchable_content` delegates to the `leafable` (e.g., `Page`, `Section`).
        For a `Page`:

        *   `markdown_source` is invoked to gather the body content.
        *   WAIT: `page.body` was set up as `has_one :markdown_body, dependent: :destroy`! The `page.markdown_body` was already DESTROYED before `after_destroy_commit`! Is `leaf.leafable` cached in memory, and specifically, is `page.markdown_body`? If `page.destroy` is run, `markdown_body` is gone. What if `leaf` was destroyed? We'll have to test this in `rails runner`.
        *   AND ALSO: What if a `User` is destroyed inside a test? If using `use_transactional_tests`, each test is wrapped in a DB transaction, or might not run correctly. messages.content: Let's test what happens to `pages`, `sections`, `pictures`, `action_text_markdowns`, `active_storage_attachments`, `active_storage_blobs`, `reading_marks`, and `edits` when a book with edits and attachments is destroyed.
messages.thinking:
**Unraveling the Persistence Puzzle**

Okay, here's what's running through my head. The key lies in understanding what *didn't* happen, as much as what did. Specifically, the prompt was about complete erasure after a `book.destroy!`, meaning no remnants should linger. The initial observation regarding the FTS row removal sparked a chain of questions.

First, let's explore all the potential points of interaction: `Leaf::Searchable`, `Book`, `Edit`, `Page`, and `Section`. I have a concern that if we use `delete_all` instead of `destroy`, the `leaf_search_index` might not be cleaned up. Also, what if `after_destroy_commit` has an `if: :searchable?` conditional? That would be a problem.

For example, imagine a `Page` with a "secret" body indexed in `leaf_search_index`. What happens when the underlying `leaf` is destroyed? The `Page` has `has_markdown :body` with `dependent: :destroy` on `ActionText::Markdown`. When the `leaf` is destroyed, the `Page` is destroyed. The `Page` then destroys its `markdown_body`, which means the `page.body` might still reference the destroyed `markdown_body` unless the page has been reloaded, or the `markdown_body` wasn't loaded to begin with!  What if `searchable_content` returns `nil` for a `Picture` or if a `Section` body is updated to `nil`, but `update_in_search_index` doesn't remove it.

But the real kicker: why is there an `if: :searchable?` condition on `after_destroy_commit :remove_from_search_index`? Deleting from `leaf_search_index where rowid = ?` for a non-existent rowid is a fast, harmless no-op in SQLite FTS5! By removing the `if: :searchable?` condition, we can guarantee absolutely no stale search hits remain for any destroyed `Leaf`. That seems like the simplest, most effective solution.

Another thought: what about `leaf_search_index` entries in `test_helper.rb` or our fixtures? I noticed in the `runner` output "FTS rows for leaf 1" and the fixtures weren't loaded in the runner.

And now, let's look at `Leaf::Editable`. I noticed `has_many :edits, dependent: :delete_all`. WAIT A SECOND. I just realized there's a big problem in `Edit` (`app/models/edit.rb`): it delegates its dependent operations.

Here's the problem: when a `Book` (or a `Leaf`) is destroyed, the `edits` rows are deleted, but the actual `leafable` records (like `Page`, `Section`, etc.) are NEVER DESTROYED! They're left orphaned in the database. This is critical. We need to verify this immediately in `bin/rails runner`. If a `Leaf` has `Edit`s (revisions or trash), and `book.destroy!` runs, the `Edit` rows are deleted, but the associated `leafable` records are left behind.

  leaf = book.press(Page.new(body: "Version 1 secret"), title: "Secret Page")
  # Simulate an older edit so a new edit creates a revision
  leaf.edit(leafable_params: { body: "Version 2 secret" }, leaf_params: { title: "Secret Page" })
  leaf.edits.last.update_columns(created_at: 1.hour.ago)

messages.thinking:
**Orphaned Records and ActiveStorage Gotchas**

Okay, here's what I'm seeing: that output is revealing a major issue! When a `book.destroy!` runs, it's leaving a bunch of orphaned records in the database, specifically `Page`, `Section`, `Picture`, `ActionText::Markdown`, and `ActiveStorage::Attachment` records that were associated with the historical edits. The issue stems from the interaction between `Leaf::Editable` having `has_many :edits, dependent: :delete_all` and `Edit` having `delegated_type :leafable, types: Leafable::TYPES, dependent: :destroy`. The `delete_all` on the `Leaf::Editable` side is bypassing the `dependent: :destroy` on the `Edit` side, leading to these orphans.

So, when a `User` is erased, we need to handle the orphaned blobs from the destroyed private books (covers, images, and, crucially, markdown uploads). **Alright, let's break down this GDPR erasure and make sure we get it right.** My immediate thought is, yes, the `everyone_access` flag is crystal clear – it’s a simple “shared with everyone” toggle. Good. Now, when Alice gets the delete hammer, a book that *is* shared with everyone remains, but it loses its creator, becomes "Deleted author", and continues to function. Bob, or anyone else, keeps their access and reading progress on that shared book. Alice's stuff gets nuked. That makes sense.

Private books, on the other hand, *poof* gone. But the cascade effect here is crucial. We're talking book, access, leaves, reading marks, edits (including all those leafables!), blobs, everything. We have to be meticulous here because, if a book *isn't* set to everyone access, we need to completely obliterate all associated data when its owner is deleted. Everything that has a *relationship* with that deleted book has to go as well.

Now, what about books where Alice had an editor role but *didn't* create?  It seems like those are safe. The model is built to ensure a foreign user's data remains untouched. That's a huge relief. However, we have to look to ensure we never write user-identifiable information into other tables.

I'm thinking, let's drill down the database schema, table by table. This is where the rubber meets the road. Accesses, books, sessions, reading marks…those seem handled. We're also using blobs, attachments and leafable objects, which need to be accounted for. We need to handle that all of the data that's only in those books is purged, including the search index.

**Okay, the `User#index` page… this is where things get interesting and where the solution might have a design benefit.** If a user gets 'removed', i.e. becomes `active: false`, should admins still see them on the `/users` page?

The issue is that we need to ensure *complete* erasure of *all* data, *even* from an admin's point of view.  Showing them on `/users` (with a clear “Remove” button) allows admins to perform the *actual* removal. If we *hide* them, we prevent complete data erasure, so we must show. The fact that the controller *does* find deactivated users for direct `DELETE` requests is a great backup. No tests would fail if they were shown, and we can make this new behavior look clean. We can add a "Deactivated" section. This will be the clearest solution, which is the only way to ensure 100% data erasure.

The test updates are also straightforward. We can make sure they are included so the tests will pass. We are going to need more tests.

Let's carefully craft a reproduction script with detailed test cases to ensure the user, and all the dependent data associated with the user, is wiped from the system correctly.

The main challenge is to think through every possible edge case before coding.

1.  We need to test users with both shared and private books, to confirm the behavior matches.
2.  We need to test the books where someone else is the creator, but Alice has editor/reader access to them.  We need to confirm those stay.
3.  We need to confirm blob sharing between shared and private resources and ensure no data loss.
4.  We must confirm the cleanup behavior with a deactivated user, so the script confirms there is no data loss.  In this scenario, we must confirm the email is the original email for all logs.
5.  Search indexing of leaves is critical.
6.  Session cleanup is easy, since we delete them using delete\_all (rather than destroy).
7.  Verify we can call `UsersController#destroy` for both active and deactivated users.
8.  Verify re-joining after deletion with the same email works as expected.
9.  We must also account for demo content and admin accounts.
10. Edits have to be dependent destroy.
11. We need to be able to purge blobs in the after\_destroy callback or we'll get stale data.

messages.content:
I have analyzed the full data model and identified all the issues to fix:
1. `UsersController#destroy` calls `@user.deactivate` instead of destroying the user, and `set_user` scopes to `User.active` which blocks erasing already-deactivated users.
2. `User::Authoring` has `dependent: :destroy` on all `created_books` (which would delete books shared with everyone instead of keeping them with `creator: nil, author: "Deleted author"`), and `has_many :reading_marks` lacks `dependent: :delete_all` (causing a foreign key violation).
3. `User` has `has_many :sessions, dependent: :destroy`, which triggers `Session::Auditable#record_signed_out` and creates a new `SignInEvent` during deletion; using `dependent: :delete_all` avoids that, and `after_destroy` must delete `SignInEvent`s for both the current `email_address` and the pre-deactivation email address (stripping `-deactivated-<uuid>`).
4. `Leaf::Editable` has `has_many :edits, dependent: :delete_all`, which orphans historical `Page`/`Section`/`Picture` leafables, `ActionText::Markdown` records, and `ActiveStorage::Attachment`s when a leaf/book is destroyed. Changing this to `dependent: :destroy` cleans them all up, and purging unreferenced blobs from destroyed private books ensures no `ActiveStorage::Blob` rows or files remain.
5. `Leaf::Searchable` uses `after_destroy_commit :remove_from_search_index, if: :searchable?`, which can miss FTS cleanup in transactions or when `searchable?` is falsy; changing it to `after_destroy :remove_from_search_index` guarantees no stale search hits remain.
6. `UsersController#index` and `app/views/users/index.html.erb` should also display deactivated users to admins so they can remove previously deactivated users from the UI.

Let's edit these files now.
messages.thinking:
**My Analysis of the Proposed Changes**

Okay, I've reviewed the proposed changes meticulously, and everything seems sound. I'm going to meticulously document my understanding of each modification and the reasoning behind them.

### `app/models/leaf/searchable.rb`

The first change focuses on how search indexes are managed. Moving from `after_destroy_commit` to `after_destroy` on the `remove_from_search_index` callback makes perfect sense. This ensures that the search index is updated *immediately* during a destroy operation, even within transactions or transactional tests, and crucially, handles edge cases where the `searchable?` guard might have failed, thus ensuring robust cleanup.

### `app/models/leaf/editable.rb` and `app/models/leaf.rb`

Here, we're shifting the `dependent` option in `has_many :edits` to `:destroy`.  This cascade will now correctly destroy the `leafable` associated with the edit (Page, Section, or Picture). The addition of `has_many :reading_marks, dependent: :delete_all` in `Leaf` is also a good addition for ActiveRecord completeness, and avoids inadvertently cascading destroys to other models.

I've traced the cascade carefully, particularly the interactions between `Edit`, `Leaf`, and `Leafable`.  Destroying a `Leaf` should correctly destroy the related `edits` and *their* `leafable`. Destroying the associated `Page` will correctly destroy its markdown, which destroys any linked attachments, which is crucial. Similarly, destroying a `Picture` will handle its attachment. I've confirmed that the destruction of `leafable` instances is correctly managed and doesn't lead to circular dependencies or orphaned data, especially in the rare cases of `touch` on `Leaf`.

### `app/models/user/authoring.rb`

This section is the most involved, but the logic is sound.  We're modifying the handling of a user's created books during user deletion.
-   Removing the `dependent: :destroy` from `has_many :created_books` is essential for `everyone_access: true` books, preventing unintended data loss.
-   The proposed `before_destroy` callback correctly handles both types of books:
    -   `everyone_access: true` books: the creator will be set to nil and the author to "Deleted author".
    -   `everyone_access: false` books: They're destroyed, and Active Storage blob IDs are collected to ensure any associated uploads are purged.
-   The order of callbacks is crucial, so I've carefully traced that.

### `app/models/user.rb`

The audit here is critical.  We're looking at the proper way to handle email address changes and deactivation of users.
-   The email address handling within `erase_sign_in_events` must be robust, and it looks like a good strategy, handling both deactivated and active emails.

### `app/controllers/users_controller.rb` and `app/views/users/index.html.erb`

I've examined the user deletion flow.
- The `index` action correctly displays active users and the deactivated users only to admins.
- The `destroy` action for both active and deactivated users looks good.  It makes sure that admins are authorized to remove users. The UI has appropriate confirmation messages.  It is robust and correctly handles edge cases, such as self-deletion and deactivation.

I've considered all the scenarios and edge cases. I'm satisfied that these changes are well-reasoned, correct, and will provide the desired behavior.

messages.thinking:
**A Deep Dive into ActiveRecord Callbacks and Unexpected Side Effects**

Okay, this is intriguing. I was just looking at how `creator_id` gets unexpectedly assigned in this system. Specifically, after updating a record with `creator_id: nil`, the ID magically reappears! That's strange. Digging deeper, I see the `Book::Authorship` module:

module Book::Authorship
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

Aha! It's the `default: -> { Current.user }` in the `belongs_to` association. I've encountered this before. Rails sets this up as a `before_validation` callback, and crucially, *it doesn't have an `on: :create` restriction.* This means that ANY time a `Book` with a `nil` `creator_id` is validated (and that happens on *every* update), the `creator_id` is silently set to `Current.user`!

That's a nasty bug waiting to happen. Consider this: Alice creates a book that everyone can access. Alice is then deleted, and the book's `creator_id` becomes `nil`. Later, Bob, an editor, updates the title. Using the current setup, that `before_validation` callback kicks in and *silently* assigns the book to Bob! We've got unintended data ownership shifts.

However, if we switch to a `before_validation :assign_creator, on: :create` (or using `optional: true` in `belongs_to` and `before_create { self.creator ||= Current.user }` or `before_validation(on: :create) { self.creator ||= Current.user }`) pattern, it behaves how one would expect:

1.  New books properly get the `creator = Current.user` on creation, just like the `default:` approach.
2.  Existing books with `creator_id = nil` (like anonymized or fixture books) *keep* `creator_id = nil` even when updated.
3.  We can directly use `book.update!(creator: nil, author: "Deleted author")` without any unexpected assignments.

Now, let's make sure no tests depend on the old behavior. I'll search the codebase to see if any tests might be relying on `Book.new.creator` before the validation/save cycle by grepping for `creator` in `test/`. The search didn't show any, which is good news!

In this situation, `Book.new.creator` would return `nil` until `valid?` or `save` because the `default:` callback uses `before_validation`, not `after_initialize` to set the value.

So, here's the refactor. Let's modify the `Book::Authorship` module:

module Book::Authorship
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

Then, in the `User::Authoring` module, when anonymizing a user's books, let's ensure we use `find_each { |book| book.update!(creator: nil, author: "Deleted author") }` with the `before_validation on: :create` setup. This is cleaner and prevents the unwanted re-attribution of the book's creator on any subsequent updates. Then, I can update the app and re-run our verification script to be absolutely sure.

    end
  end
end
